title: Why Are We Still Prescribing Most Oral Medicines for Depression in Adolescents?
subtitle: It makes close to no sense to this psychiatrist
body_html:
The greatest trick the devil ever played? Something that had good branding, I assume. Today, I take another pass at one of my favorite topics—the ubiquity of oral medicines in the treatment of adolescent depression, and their startling lack of efficacy. At the same time, we have effective treatments that work better, safer, and faster.

To bring readers up to speed, only Prozac (fluoxetine) has evidence (among pills) for antidepressant efficacy in youth.

“At this point, we’d like to read you the list of antidepressants that did not pass muster in youth depression, but it’s too long. Suffice it to say that it includes the tricyclics and nearly all modern antidepressants – including the newest ones, levomilnacipran, vilazodone, and vortioxetine – just about all except trazodone and bupropion. Those are still uncharted territory. So, outside of fluoxetine, why do we use antidepressants in children?”

KELLIE NEWSOME, On The Carlat Psychiatry Podcast.

And yet, in 2022, the most recent year in which we have US data, we collectively suborned the prescription of 9.44M non-fluoxetine oral antidepressants to youth 12-17.1

To be very clear, those medicines only added risk, not benefit.

It is back-of-the-envelope math that excludes all the kids 0-11 who were also prescribed those meds. We thus have somewhere over 10,000,000 prescriptions written, with an FDA black box warning for increasing suicidal ideation.

Well, I’d argue we need to do four things for kids and families, now:

  1. Child Psychiatrists and Pediatricians should become OBSESSED with deprescribing those drugs. It is a reasonable strategy for both safety and risk management. Any family with a bad outcome— there are 700,000 suicide attempts among adolescents in 2024—can and will start suing and winning. The last prescriber in holding the hot-potato, and who who didn’t document a plan for deprescribing? I wouldn’t want to be an underwriter. If you want more info on deprescribing of antidepressants, check out Outro Health.

  2. Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation has an FDA label for adolescent depression, and national coverage from UnitedHealthgroup, Cigna, Medical, and more for heaven’s sake. Other plans will follow. It’s safe and effective and should be a first line treatment along with general psychiatric management in suicidal youth.

  3. Psychotherapy without antidepressants (plus TMS when needed) should be the standard in suicidal youth. That means physicians either LEARNING therapy themselves or working with therapists in teams, or both. I even wrote a therapy manual on the topic myself, to help— get “Adolescent Suicide and Self-Injury: Mentalizing Theory and Treatment” here (amazon affiliate link).

  4. Stop kidding ourselves, and start working—hard, and now—on more effective options such as TMS for adolescents. We have myriad treatments in the pipeline for adults, lets ask regulators to offer label extensions if study sponsors do pediatric trials, or something of similar value. We need to incentive novel therapeutic and payment models for kids.

Thanks for coming to my talk. If you want more of this concise, actionable insight on the future of Brain Medicine, I hope you will be in San Fransisco for JPM!
